title: Koyasan
hookLine: Kukai founds Shingon on Mount Koya; pilgrims still walk his island route

cards: On the island of Shikoku, a walker in white sets off down a country road with a wooden staff and a wide sedge hat. No one else is in sight. Still, pilgrims on this road have a phrase for it: two traveling together.
One is the walker. The other, they say, is Kukai, the monk whose memory this long loop of temples carries. The staff, in their telling, stands for him.
So the walker is never quite alone.

teach.h: KUKAI BRINGS HOME A TRUE WORD.
teach.b: Kukai was a Japanese monk who, his biographies say, sailed to China to study and came home with an esoteric teaching that works through body, speech and mind at once: hands shaped into gestures, sacred sounds chanted, the mind resting on a figure of the Buddha.
His school took the name Shingon, true word, after the mantras at its heart.
He taught at court in the capital, where a great temple was later put in his care. But he also wanted a place apart, far from politics, for meditation.

So he asked the emperor for a mountain, a high valley ringed by peaks, and on Mount Koya he began a monastery. Koyasan. Over time it grew into a town of temples, with halls, monks, and a forest of graves under old cedars.
Here the history turns into faith. Kukai came to be honored by the title Kobo Daishi.

teach.h: TRADITION SAYS HE IS STILL SITTING.
teach.b: Tradition says he did not die on the mountain but entered deep meditation, and is still sitting there in the inner sanctuary. Monks, tradition says, still bring meals to his hall.
Shingon followers hold this in different ways: some take it plainly, some as a way of saying his teaching is alive. Either way, the road matters.

Pilgrims walk the temple loop on Shikoku, his home island, on foot, by bus, or a section at a time, and some finish by climbing to Koyasan to give thanks. The temples are known; the pilgrim isn't discovering anything new.

teach.h: THE ROAD ITSELF IS THE PRACTICE.
teach.b: The road itself is the practice.
One step, one temple, one bow, and, in the pilgrims' telling, the companion walking beside them is the one they came to meet.

how: Pilgrims walk the Shikoku temple circuit associated with Kukai, often dressed in white with a staff and a sedge hat, and some also climb to Koyasan to pay respects at his mausoleum.

games.q: you're Kukai, home from China with a new teaching and busy at court. you want a place apart for meditation. what do you ask for?
o: a bigger hall in the capital.
a monastery on a remote mountain.
games.why: Kukai asked for Mount Koya, a high valley ringed by peaks. it grew into a town of temples that pilgrims still climb to.

practice: If you can stand, walk slowly to a window or a doorway and back, and at the far end lower your head or stop for one breath; if you can't walk right now, trace the route with your eyes.
Then sit and let the walk go on inside, one step, one breath, with someone walking beside you if you'd like a companion.

wordCard.voice: Koyasan. Mount Koya, where Kukai made a home for his Shingon school, and where, tradition says, he still sits in meditation.

orig.note: Sanskrit mantra, a sacred sound. Shingon, the name of Kukai's school, means true word, after the mantras at its heart.

carryVoice: Your line: the pilgrim's road. On it, no one walks quite alone. Until tomorrow.
